about.lede: Softcom is a technology and innovation company with 19 years of experience building digital products, enterprise systems and large-scale initiatives for public institutions, private organisations and development enablers.

about.convictionTitle: Built from conviction about Africa’s potential.
conviction: Softcom was founded in 2007 with a mission to give many people a path to growth, achievement and fulfilment.

When technology was largely associated with global giants, solving an everyday problem with software showed us what was possible. We took that same approach into enterprises: understand what they wanted to achieve and build the answers they needed.
Today, our mission remains the same: to help organisations, our people and the communities we reach achieve more. Their progress gives purpose to ours.

milestones.title: Pioneering electronic airtime purchases
milestones.body: Founded in 2007, Softcom was among the pioneers of electronic airtime purchasing in Nigeria. ReloadNG enabled people to purchase airtime online, through a text message or with a missed call, introducing new ways to access an everyday service.

milestones.title: Enterprise systems and industry value chains
milestones.body: Softcom developed enterprise systems across FMCG and financial services. The work deepened the company’s understanding of industry value chains and how technology could support operations, distribution and service delivery.

milestones.title: Deepening our footprint in education
milestones.body: The Future Ready University conference brought Softcom together with university leaders, opening relationships that led to technology engagements across the education sector.

milestones.title: A landmark in national development
milestones.body: Working with the Bank of Industry, Softcom delivered technology supporting the recruitment, training, deployment, management and payment of more than 500,000 graduates.

milestones.title: Pioneering banking with a phone number
milestones.body: Softcom developed Eyowo, pioneering a way for consumers to bank using their existing phone numbers. Removing the leading zero turned the remaining ten digits into an account number. The platform went on to reach more than 4.5 million users.

milestones.title: A landmark in development finance
milestones.body: Softcom’s technology enabled delivery of microloans to more than 1.2 million traders across Nigeria, most of whom were previously unbanked.

milestones.title: Platforms enabling new services
milestones.body: Softcom launched platforms enabling services across data, stateless payments, retail and banking, giving organisations digital foundations through which to serve their customers and users.

milestones.title: Web3, AI and machine learning
milestones.body: Our work expanded into systems using Web3 technologies and intelligence solutions powered by artificial intelligence and machine learning.

milestones.title: Nineteen years of technology and innovation
milestones.body: Softcom’s work spans Digital Infrastructure, Applied Intelligence and Powering Initiatives, bringing proprietary technology, partner platforms and delivery expertise to public institutions, private organisations and development enablers.

sections.title: The more a member verifies, the more opens.
sections.body: A new member browses. A verified individual learns, attends and buys. A verified business sells, lists, applies for funding and advertises. A business with a good record earns Trusted status, and keeps it only while the record holds.

sections.title: Six things a business needs, one account.
sections.body: Most initiatives offer training on one site, grants on another and a directory nobody updates. LIFT puts six modules behind one profile: Learn, Connect, Trade, Finance, Register and Grow. A member who verifies for the marketplace is already verified for a grant, a directory listing and a trademark search.

sections.title: Verify in stages, not all at once.
sections.body: Sign-up asks for a name, a phone number, an email and a national identification number. Identity verification is automated. Business verification checks registration, tax identification and documents, is reviewed by people, and takes two to three working days. Nothing is asked for before it is needed.

sections.title: Funding that members can see, and reach.
sections.body: Grant and loan programmes from government agencies, development banks and financial institutions are listed in one place, with amounts, eligibility and closing dates. A verified business applies with most of the form already filled from their profile.

sections.title: A marketplace, a directory, and a community.
sections.body: Members buy from each other. Payment is held by the platform until the buyer confirms delivery. Every verified business gets a listing it maintains itself. Events, courses and a forum sit in the same account.

sections.title: Built to be run, not just launched.
sections.body: The sponsoring organisation publishes programmes, events and resources, reviews business verifications, sees applications as they arrive, and reports on reach. The tiers, modules and rules are shared. The brand, colour, type and content are configuration, so a state ministry and a national agency can each run LIFT as their own initiative.

items.name: Reckon
items.headline: What was declared vs what is owed.
items.lede: A tax return says what a company declared. The documents filed show what is owed. Reckon reads every one of those documents, works out the tax each line should have attracted, and shows the officer where the two disagree.
items.summary: Audit beyond the limits of manual review.

image.label: Reckon · Hero
image.alt: Records and evidence laid out for review

sections.title: Most of what is missed was never looked for.
sections.body: A liability rarely hides in one document. It shows where the general ledger, the bank statement and the return disagree, and those three are seldom put side by side. Reckon compares every line, so a check that takes an officer a week happens in seconds.

sections.title: Start with what the taxpayer already filed.
sections.body: Returns, general ledgers, trial balances, financial statements, schedules and bank statements, in PDF, Excel or scanned form. Reckon reads them into one chart of accounts and maps every line to the tax areas it falls under.

sections.title: Every line, tested.
sections.body: For each line Reckon classifies what it is, computes what the applicable rule expects, and compares that with what was declared and what was remitted. A fee posted to the interest ledger is still a fee, and is tested as one. Differences above the materiality threshold become exceptions.

sections.title: The officer decides.
sections.body: Reckon raises exceptions; it does not raise findings. Every exception is reviewed by an officer, who raises a finding or dismisses it with a reason. The rules are configuration the administration maintains, so two teams examining the same taxpayer reach the same result.

sections.title: One engine. Desk review, audit, investigation.
sections.body: Desk review runs on every filing as it arrives. Audit takes selected cases through evidence requests, fieldwork and findings. Investigation works at transaction level. The rules and the taxpayer record are shared.

items.audienceTitle: Built for those with a mandate to collect.
items.audienceBody: Revenue administrations and large-taxpayer offices, state internal revenue services, tax audit and investigation units, and the audit firms acting for them.
items.close: Tell us which filings you review and what your audits need to establish. We will run Reckon on records you select, against criteria you set.

insights.headline: Research, analysis, perspectives from the field.
insights.lede: Thinking from Softcom's practice leads, on digital transformation, data strategy, government technology, and the forces shaping Africa's technology landscape.

items.title: Why Digital Transformation Fails in African Enterprises — And What to Do About It
items.excerpt: Most digital transformation efforts fail not because of bad technology, but because of a fundamental misreading of what needs to change.

image.label: Insight · Digital transformation
image.alt: Hands reviewing photographs and notes on a wooden table

paragraphs: Across Nigeria and the broader African continent, the story repeats itself with uncomfortable regularity. A large enterprise — bank, telco, retailer, or government agency — announces a major digital transformation initiative. External consultants are brought in. A global platform is selected. Millions are committed. And then, two or three years later, the system sits half-implemented, the champions have moved on, and the organisation reverts to what it was doing before.

The failure is rarely technological. The platforms being deployed — whether ERP systems, core banking software, CRM tools, or data platforms — are mature, tested, and capable. The failure is almost always organisational. It is a failure to change the workflows, incentive structures, and mental models that the technology is supposed to serve. A digital system layered onto an analogue process does not produce a digital process. It produces an expensive, underused system and a frustrated workforce.

There are three patterns we see most consistently in failed transformations. The first is scope without sequence — organisations try to change everything at once and end up changing nothing. The second is technology without redesign — new tools are deployed without rethinking the underlying processes they are supposed to improve. The third is implementation without ownership — transformation programmes are run by external teams with no accountability for outcomes after go-live.

What works is different. Successful transformations in African enterprises share a common thread: they start small, move deliberately, and are owned internally at a senior level. They treat the first phase as a learning exercise, not a solution deployment. They build internal capability alongside external delivery. And they define success not by go-live, but by measurable improvement in operational outcomes — faster service, lower cost, better decisions.

For Softcom, this insight has shaped how we engage. We do not sell transformation as a destination. We design it as a journey — one with clear phases, internal champions, and outcomes we stay accountable for long after the initial deployment.

items.title: Building a Data Culture: Lessons from Nigeria’s Financial Sector
items.excerpt: Nigerian financial institutions do not lack data. They lack a shared habit of using it when a decision is actually made.

image.label: Insight · Data culture
image.alt: A team reading evidence on screen

paragraphs: Nigerian financial institutions do not lack data. They lack a shared habit of using it. Reports multiply, dashboards launch, and the decisions that matter still travel by experience, hierarchy and the last meeting in the room.

A data culture is not a platform. It is the agreement, repeated in ordinary work, that a claim should be traceable, a number should have an owner, and a team should be able to ask a harder question than the one the report was built to answer. Technology can make that possible. It cannot make it normal.

The institutions that move usually start inside a single decision, not a transformation programme. They pick a question leadership already cares about, put the evidence next to the people who decide, and stay with the workflow until the new habit is cheaper than the old one.
